studies.title: Made, And Then Divided
studies.meaning: The surah opens the way several others do, with everything in the heavens and the earth glorifying God, and then adds two possessions and a capacity: the kingdom, the praise, and power over everything. The second ayah narrows sharply. The same creator made you, and among you there is one who rejects and one who believes. The grammar is singular on both sides, so the split is drawn between persons rather than parties. The closing clause is not about belief at all: God sees what you do.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, though the classical sources record disagreement about this surah, with some holding parts of it Meccan. It is the last of the group of chapters that open by declaring the glorification of God, and the only one of them that turns immediately to a division among human beings. No occasion is reported for these two ayat. The commentators read them as the frame for everything that follows about testing, loss and gain.

keyTerms.note: A noun for possession that carries the right to dispose, not merely to own. Placed with the definite article and no qualifier, it claims the whole of sovereignty rather than a share of it.
The root means to cover, and it is used of a farmer burying seed and of night hiding the land. Rejection is pictured as concealing something already present rather than as lacking it.
A divine name for sight that discerns rather than merely registers. It closes an ayah about belief with a statement about conduct, which pairs the inward division with something observable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Kingship was an idea Arabians knew mostly from a distance. The peninsula had no crown of its own; the kings were in Persia and in the Byzantine provinces to the north, and caravans returned with accounts of courts, taxes and the reach of a distant throne. Tribal Arabia had chiefs instead, whose authority ended at the edge of their people. A claim to hold the whole kingdom landed against that contrast.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that opens this surah appears in the present tense, while the same opening line in three earlier surahs uses the past. Reciters hear the difference immediately: three chapters report that glorification happened, and two, including this one, say it is happening. The Quran otherwise rarely varies a repeated formula in this way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat together make a claim that is harder than either alone. God is named as the creator of everyone, and then belief and rejection are both located inside that creation without the creator being divided from either outcome. The Quran does not resolve this here and the commentators do not force it, holding together divine power and human responsibility. What the passage does add is the closing clause, which returns the question to what people actually do.

crossReferences.why: States that the way was shown and the human being is then either grateful or ungrateful.
Describes the soul as given both its wrongdoing and its awareness of what is right.
Says each person acts according to his disposition, and God knows best who is better guided.

studies.applyIt: Spend one hour today doing something small that nobody will see: a repair, a message, a debt paid quietly. The ayah pairs the deepest division between people, belief and its refusal, with a closing line about ordinary conduct. That pairing suggests a scale on which the invisible hour counts, which is worth testing rather than assuming.

studies.title: Shaped, And Shaped Well
studies.meaning: Three statements in one line, moving from the largest scale to the smallest and then past both. The heavens and the earth were made with truth, which the commentators gloss as purpose rather than accuracy: made for something, not made accidentally. Then the same verb narrows to human beings, who are given form and given it well. The word for form covers face and figure together. The line closes by naming the destination, so the shaping is placed inside a journey rather than presented as an end.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah belongs to the surah's opening argument, which establishes who is speaking before it asks anything of the reader. The commentators report no occasion. They note instead that the statement about human form appears in more than one surah with slight variations, and read its presence here as preparing the passage about testing that comes later, since a form given well raises the question of what it is for.

keyTerms.note: The word covers truth, right and reality at once. Used of creation it says the making was not play or accident, which is how the classical commentators consistently gloss it wherever the phrase occurs.

An intensive verb for giving shape to something already made, distinct from the verb for bringing it into being. The order is deliberate: creation first, then the individual features that make one person unlike another.
From a verb meaning to become, so the word means both the place you arrive at and the thing you turn into. Arabic keeps those two ideas in one noun, which English needs two words for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Craft was visible work in that world. A potter shaped a jar on a wheel where anyone passing could watch, a smith beat a blade into its curve, a leatherworker cut a waterskin to fit a saddle. The vocabulary of forming belonged to those trades before it belonged to theology. Hearing that God formed you well would have carried the sense a buyer has picking up good work: made by someone who cared how it came out.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that God formed you and formed you well appears twice in the Quran with nearly identical wording, here and in a later surah. The verb behind it, giving shape, is also the source of the ordinary Arabic word for a picture or an image, so the same root covers both the forming of a body and the making of a likeness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Purpose is asserted twice in one line, once about the cosmos and once about the individual, and the second is the harder claim. Saying that the universe was made for something is a large statement that costs a reader nothing personally. Saying that your particular face and frame were shaped, and shaped well, puts the same claim inside a body you may not like. The closing word then prevents the compliment from becoming a resting place.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the phrase about forming you and forming you well, adding good provision to it.
States that the human being was created in the best of statures, using a different word for the idea.
Asks whether you thought you were created without purpose and would not be returned.

studies.applyIt: Look at your own face in a mirror for ten seconds longer than is comfortable, without fixing anything. Most people run a commentary there. The ayah says the shaping was done well and then immediately names where you are going, which is a way of saying that the face matters and is not the point. Try holding both at once.

studies.title: What You Hide And Show
studies.meaning: Knowledge is described in circles that narrow until they close on the reader. First what is in the heavens and the earth, then the two categories of human action, concealed and declared, and finally what is in the chests, which the commentators take as intention rather than passing thought. The order reverses the usual direction of a description: it starts with the vast and finishes with the private. The word for chests is used rather than hearts, keeping the image physical, a place things are kept rather than a faculty.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and placed in a surah that will shortly describe people whose outward conduct and inward position did not match. The ayah arrives before that description rather than after it, which the commentators read as deliberate: the standard is stated generally before anyone is measured by it. No specific occasion is reported. The phrase about what is in the chests recurs across the Quran in similar positions.

keyTerms.note: A verb for concealing deliberately, from a root that also gives the words for a secret and for gladness kept private. It implies something held back by choice rather than merely unspoken.
The paired opposite, meaning to bring into the open where others can see. Naming both halves leaves no third category, so the ayah covers everything a person does without listing anything.

The plural of the word for the chest, used across the Quran as the place where intentions are stored. Choosing it over the word for heart keeps the picture concrete, like a container whose contents are known from outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Privacy was thin in a seventh-century settlement. Houses shared walls, courtyards were common ground, and a conversation at the well travelled the length of the town by evening. What people could genuinely keep hidden was small: a grudge, an intention, a plan not yet acted on. The ayah goes straight to that narrow margin, which was the only place anyone had left, and says it is not a margin at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about God knowing what is within the chests occurs more than a dozen times in the Quran, almost always as a closing clause and rarely as the main statement of a sentence. It functions as a seal rather than an argument, which is why it tends to arrive after a passage about speech, secrecy or dispute rather than before one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Divine knowledge is presented here as continuous rather than as inspection at intervals, which changes what privacy means. If nothing is unobserved, then concealment is not a failed strategy but a category error. The passage also refuses to separate the cosmic from the personal: the same clause that covers the heavens covers the thought you have not said. That equivalence is the point, and it is offered without threat attached.

crossReferences.why: Says what is in yourselves, whether disclosed or hidden, will be brought to account by God.
States that God knows the secret and whatever is more hidden than a secret.
Makes no difference between one who conceals his speech and one who declares it openly.

studies.applyIt: Write down, for yourself only, the real reason behind something you did this week that you gave a better reason for. Do not show it to anyone and do not fix it. The ayah is not asking for confession. It is pointing out that the private version already exists somewhere, fully stated, and that you are the only one avoiding reading it.

studies.title: Has The News Not Reached You
studies.meaning: The question is rhetorical but its form matters: the reader is asked whether a report has arrived, not whether a claim is true. That puts the burden on memory rather than on argument. The tense then splits. Earlier peoples tasted the consequence of their own affair, a past event, and a painful punishment is waiting, a future one. Commentators note that the word for consequence carries the sense of something heavy and indigestible, so the outcome is described as the weight of a thing already swallowed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah has just established God's knowledge and power; this is the first place it turns outward to history. Arabia had physical evidence of vanished peoples, ruins on the trade routes north and south that caravans passed without stopping. The commentators do not attach an occasion to the ayah. They note that the question assumes the audience already knows the stories, which the ruins and the poets had kept in circulation.

keyTerms.note: Not ordinary news. The word is used of reports that carry consequence and are worth acting on, which is why it names the accounts of earlier communities rather than daily information.
A verb of direct sensation rather than of knowing. Tasting is the most immediate form of learning, and using it for consequence says the lesson arrived through experience and not through being told.
A word for something heavy and hard to digest, used of food that sits badly and of rain that damages. Applied to conduct it makes the result a property of the act rather than a separate penalty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The caravan road from Mecca northward ran past standing evidence of the past. Rock-cut facades in the valleys of the north, abandoned wells, the outlines of settlements that had once controlled a route and no longer existed. Travellers named them and told the stories at night camps, and the poets used them as a stock image for the passing of everything. A question about news that had reached you was partly a question about what you had walked past.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about tasting the consequence of one's own affair appears in the Quran three times, in three different surahs, each time about earlier communities and each time in the past tense. The near-identical repetition is a feature of the Quran's historical passages, where a fixed formula marks the same pattern recurring in different peoples.
studies.theologicalSignificance: History is treated as evidence rather than as decoration, which sets a particular relationship between the reader and the past. The claim is not merely that certain peoples were punished; it is that a pattern is visible and has been reported, and that refusing to look at it is itself a choice. The ayah also divides the outcome across two times, something already tasted and something still ahead, which keeps the present from feeling settled.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same sentence about tasting the consequence of one's own affair, about a nearer example.
Tells the reader to travel the earth and look at how those who came before them ended.
Opens with the same question about whether the news of earlier peoples has reached them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a pattern in your own family or workplace that has already played out once, with someone else. You know how it went. Write the ending down in a sentence and put it where you will see it this week. The ayah does not ask you to fear anything. It asks whether the report reached you, and whether you did anything with it.

studies.title: Are Human Beings To Guide Us
studies.meaning: The objection quoted is one sentence long and the Quran treats it as the whole of the case. Messengers came with clear evidence, and the answer given was a question about their species: are mortals going to guide us. Commentators read this as the recurring obstacle across every prophetic mission, the expectation that a message from God should not arrive through someone who eats and sleeps. The ayah then adds a clause that is easy to miss. God had no need of them, and the ayah's two closing names restate it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, though the objection quoted belongs to the Meccan years and to every earlier mission the Quran describes. The commentators do not attach a specific occasion. They read the ayah as a summary of a standing argument: opponents in Mecca had asked why an angel was not sent instead, and the same complaint is reported of the peoples of Noah, Hud and Salih. The Quran answers it by pointing at the audience rather than at the messenger.

keyTerms.note: The word for a human being seen as flesh, from a root meaning skin. It is the term the Quran uses when the physical nature of a person is the issue, which is exactly what the objection turns on.

A verb meaning to find oneself without need of something. Used of God after a rejection, it removes the idea that refusal costs Him anything, which is a different consolation from saying the refusal will be punished.

A name meaning worthy of praise whether or not praise is given. Pairing it with self-sufficiency completes the point: the value described does not depend on recognition, so withholding recognition changes nothing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Arabia came with visible markers: age, lineage, wealth, the number of men a family could field. A claim to speak for God from someone whose father, trade and debts everyone knew was socially awkward in a way that is hard to reconstruct now. Neighbours had watched the man grow up. The objection in this ayah is not sophisticated philosophy; it is the reaction of a small town to one of its own.
studies.didYouKnow: The complaint that a messenger is only a human being appears in the Quran in the mouths of several different peoples, separated by centuries, and the wording stays close each time. The Quran presents it as the most persistent objection to prophecy, more common in its pages than any argument about the content of the message itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Quran answers this objection elsewhere by pointing out what a messenger who was not human would fail to do. A message delivered by someone who cannot be tired, hungry or bereaved could be believed but not followed, since following requires a life shaped like yours. The second half of this ayah moves in the opposite direction, insisting that God gains nothing from being believed. Together they place the whole stake on the human side.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same objection by saying angels would have been sent if angels walked the earth.
Quotes messengers replying that they are indeed human like their people, sent by God's favour.
States that earlier messengers were not bodies exempt from eating, nor were they immortal.

studies.applyIt: Notice who you discount because you know too much about them: the sibling, the colleague whose first job you remember, the friend who was wrong about something years ago. Ask one of them, this week, about a thing they genuinely understand better than you, and listen without correcting. The objection in this ayah is about familiarity, not about evidence.

studies.title: An Oath About The Rising
studies.meaning: The messenger is told to answer a denial with an oath, and the subject sworn to is the resurrection. The denial is introduced with a verb the Quran uses for unsupported assertion, and the reply begins with a particle that contradicts a negative, so the exchange is built like an argument in a courtyard. What follows the oath is not a description of the event but of its content: you will be informed of what you did. Then a clause that reduces the scale entirely, calling it easy. The second ayah turns from argument to invitation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Resurrection was the point on which the Meccan opposition had been most confident, treating the return of scattered bones as self-evidently impossible, and the argument travelled with the community to Medina. The commentators report no single occasion here. They note the shape of the passage instead: a denial, an oath, a consequence and then an invitation, which is the sequence the Quran uses whenever the dispute is about the last day.

keyTerms.note: A particle used only to contradict a negative statement, where the ordinary word for yes would be ambiguous. Arabic keeps a separate word for this, so the reply overturns the denial rather than merely disagreeing with it.

A word for something requiring little effort, used of a small matter or an easy road. Applied to raising the dead it answers an objection about difficulty by denying that difficulty is a category that applies.

The revelation is named as light rather than as a book, which is how the Quran often describes itself at moments of invitation. The word puts the emphasis on what it lets you see rather than on what it contains.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths in Arabia were serious instruments and people swore by what they valued: their fathers, their idols, the life of a son. Swearing falsely was believed to bring ruin on a household, and men declined to swear rather than risk it even when they were in the right. A messenger instructed to swear by his Lord was therefore staking everything he had on a claim about the future, in a form his listeners could weigh exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran instructs the messenger to swear by his Lord in only three places, and all three answer a denial of the same thing: that the last day is coming. Each begins with the particle that contradicts a negative, and each is followed by a statement about what will then be known. The formula is almost identical across the three.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about difficulty that reorganises the argument. Opponents treated resurrection as a question of feasibility, and the reply does not offer a mechanism; it says the matter is easy, which removes feasibility from the discussion altogether. The invitation that follows names three objects of belief in one breath: God, the messenger and the revelation, with the last called light, so acceptance is framed as coming into visibility.

crossReferences.why: Contains one of the two parallel oaths, sworn about the hour, in nearly identical wording.
Answers the objection about decayed bones by naming the one who produced them the first time.
Calls the revelation a clear light sent down to humanity, the same description used here.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you say you believe about the future and ask what you would do differently today if it were certain. Then do one small piece of that thing. The ayah does not argue anyone into the last day; it stakes an oath on it and moves straight to a statement about conduct. Belief here is measured in what changes on Tuesday.

studies.title: The Day Of Mutual Loss
studies.meaning: The surah takes its name from a single word in this ayah, and the word is commercial. It describes what happens in a trade when one side discovers afterwards that the exchange went against them. Applied to the day of gathering, it means every person will see what their choices actually bought. Commentators note that the form used is reciprocal, so the loss and gain run in both directions at once: the same transaction that one party regrets, another is glad of. What follows is the promise attached to belief and good work.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah's audience were traders and farmers who settled accounts constantly and knew the particular feeling the name describes: the moment after a deal closes when you learn what the other party knew. The commentators do not report an occasion for this ayah. They point to its placement, immediately after an invitation to believe, so the naming of the day arrives as the consequence of the choice just offered.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form from a root meaning to get the better of someone in a bargain. It names the discovery of a bad deal, and its reciprocal shape means both sides find out at the same moment.

A noun for bringing scattered things together, used of a crowd, a harvest and a sum in arithmetic. Placing it beside the word for the day makes assembly itself the defining event rather than the judgement that follows.

An intensive verb meaning to cover something so it no longer shows, from the same root as the word for rejecting faith. Wrongs are described as concealed rather than erased, which is a quieter promise than cancellation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Markets in that world ran on judgement rather than on labels. A buyer assessed a camel by its teeth and its gait, dates by weight and smell, cloth by the feel of the weave, and the seller knew things the buyer did not. Disputes afterwards were common and had their own vocabulary. A man who had been outmanoeuvred used the very word this surah is named for, and everyone knew which sensation was meant.
studies.didYouKnow: The word that names this surah occurs only once in the whole Quran, here, and it is one of a small number of surah titles taken from a word used a single time. The Quran gives the last day many names, and the classical commentators list dozens of them: the day of gathering, the day of reckoning, the day of regret, the overwhelming, the striking.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the last day after a commercial disappointment is a striking choice. It frames judgement not as a sentence handed down but as a valuation finally made visible, which means nothing new happens on that day except clarity. That has a consequence the commentators draw out: the loss described is not inflicted, it is discovered. What was traded away was traded away at the time, in ordinary hours, by people who thought they were gaining.

crossReferences.why: Names the same event the day of assembly, with people divided into two groups when it comes.
Calls the true losers those who lose themselves and their families on the day of resurrection.
States that whoever is kept from the fire and admitted to the garden has won, and this life deceives.

studies.applyIt: Look at one recurring expense of your time this month, not money: the scroll, the argument you keep having, the show you finish without wanting to. Work out the hours. Then decide whether you would make that trade again knowing the price. The word this surah is named for describes exactly that calculation, done too late.

studies.title: The Other Half Of The Sentence
studies.meaning: The counterpart to the previous ayah, and the symmetry is exact enough to be worth noticing: two conditions there, two here, a destination each way, and a verdict on each. Rejection is paired with calling the signs lies, which distinguishes refusal from ignorance. The word for the people of the fire is the ordinary word for companions, the same word used of travellers who share a road. And the closing phrase repeats a noun from earlier in the surah, where the destination was first named without content.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Pairs of this kind, one ayah for each outcome, run through the Medinan surahs and had a practical function in a community that recited them aloud together. The commentators report no occasion. They note that the surah has now completed its argument: creation, knowledge, history, resurrection, and the two ends. What follows turns entirely to the reader's own household.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb meaning to declare something false, not merely to doubt it. Pairing it with rejection makes the position active: the signs were received, assessed and publicly contradicted.

The everyday word for people who keep company, used of friends, of a caravan and of the men around a chief. Applied to the fire it makes the relation one of long association rather than of confinement.

A participle for remaining without end, which in older Arabic could simply mean lasting a very long time. The neighbouring ayah adds a separate word for perpetuity to it; here the participle stands alone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fire in that setting was daily and mostly benign: the cooking hearth, the signal fire on a hill, the flame kept alive overnight so it would not have to be struck again at dawn. Fire was also the thing everyone had been burned by at least once. It was not an abstraction borrowed for effect. Hearing it named as a companion would have joined something ordinary to something feared.
studies.didYouKnow: The construction that calls people the companions of the fire appears dozens of times in the Quran, and the matching phrase for the garden appears almost as often. Arabic has other ways to say inhabitant or prisoner; the Book consistently chooses the word for the people you travel and sit with, on both sides of the pairing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah names two conditions rather than one, and the second is the decisive addition. Disbelief alone is not what is described; it is joined to an active denial of signs that had arrived. That distinction runs through the Quran and keeps the category from covering anyone who has not been reached. What the passage establishes is that the outcome follows a response, and a response requires something to respond to.

crossReferences.why: Pairs rejection with denying the signs and names the same outcome, in almost the same construction.
States that God does not punish until a messenger has been sent, which limits the category described here.
Describes repentance accepted from those who do wrong in ignorance and then turn back soon after.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you know to be true and have arranged your life not to look at: a health result, a bank balance, a relationship you are letting cool. The ayah distinguishes not knowing from knowing and denying. Look at the thing this week, for five minutes, without deciding anything. Looking is the whole of the exercise.

studies.title: The Heart Guided Under Blows
studies.meaning: The first clause states that nothing strikes without permission, and then does something the reader may not expect: instead of explaining why, it describes an effect. Whoever believes in God has his heart guided. The classical readers gloss that guidance concretely, as being brought to say the words of return and to stay steady. So the passage does not answer the question about suffering. It says what belief does inside a person while the answer is unavailable.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah that speaks to a mixed audience. All through it, the subject is what people do with what happens to them. No set occasion is reported for these ayat. The surah is named for a day of shared loss and gain. This passage sits between that scene and rules about family and property. So a line about disaster lands in the middle of ordinary life.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to hit a target. The word carries aim rather than chance, which is why the ayah can say it happens by leave without adding to the image.
What is guided is the heart, not the person and not the path. Early scholars take it as steadiness under the blow, rather than an explanation handed over afterwards.
A verb of naming someone to act on your behalf, from the same root as an agent or a proxy. It names a handover of the outcome, not a lack of effort.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disaster in seventh-century Arabia came with no warning and no remedy. A child died of a fever in two days. A well turned salty. A raid took a herd. There was no insurance, no medicine and no court to appeal to. People carried their losses in poetry, because there was nowhere else to put them. A line saying that nothing lands without God's leave met an audience with nothing else to hold on to.
studies.didYouKnow: The old commentaries keep an early gloss on the phrase about the guided heart. A companion gave it. He said it means the man who, when something strikes him, knows it came from God and settles into that. The gloss is short, and it has been carried ever since, largely because the Quran leaves the phrase open.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's leave and a steady heart are set in one sentence, with no argument drawn from one to the other. The passage does not say that pain is good, or earned, or open to explanation. What it offers is a change in the person, not in the event. The call to obey that follows has a limit of its own. The messenger's job is to deliver the message. What comes of it is not on him either.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the words the classical readers hear inside the guided heart, spoken at the moment of the blow.
States the same permission in the language of a written record, in a passage about not grieving.
Puts the same claim in the mouths of believers as a reply, rather than stating it as doctrine.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last thing that went badly for you. Notice which question you asked first: why did this happen, or what do I do now. Neither is wrong. But the ayah offers only the second kind of help. People who keep asking the first often wait a long time for an answer this passage does not promise.
studies.explainEasier: Nothing bad happens unless God allows it. God does not explain why. He says that if you trust him, he will steady your heart while it happens. Then he tells people to obey him and to lean on him.

studies.title: Beware, Then Pardon
studies.meaning: A hard word is used, then softened at once. Some among your spouses and children are called enemies. A small particle meaning some of limits the claim, so it is not all of them, and the warning is to be wary rather than to act. Then three words for pardon come in a row, each a little different. The ayah ends on God's forgiving, not on the danger. The next line makes the whole thing a test.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan by placement, though early scholars report an occasion in Mecca. Men wanted to emigrate. Their wives and children did not want to leave and held them back. Those men later found that the ones who went ahead had learned more of the religion. The report comes from an early authority, and the sources agree on it reasonably well. It explains the word enemy without stretching it past that case.

keyTerms.note: The word is singular here and has no article, and it follows a particle meaning some of. Both features narrow it, so the ayah describes a situation that can arise rather than a type of person.
From the word for the flat face of a thing, so the image is turning your page or your cheek away from the wrong. It is the middle of three verbs, stronger than pardon and short of forgiving.
The same word used of testing metal in fire. Calling wealth and children a test says nothing about whether they are good. It says they show what a person is made of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Emigration split households. A man leaving Mecca left a business, a clan and often a wife's family who had every reason to keep him. Some who went travelled alone and did not see their children for years. Arab marriage tied two families together, so a decision like that broke more than a home. The people who first heard this ayah could name the relatives who had tried to stop them.
studies.didYouKnow: Three different verbs for letting an offence go are stacked in one clause. The Quran does that only here. Two of them turn up together elsewhere. The third is the word usually kept for God's own forgiving, and adding it is what makes the run unusual. The ayah then closes by giving that same verb to God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage holds a real conflict open instead of settling it either way. The danger is named honestly. A reader does not have to pretend that the people closest to them never stand in the way. The answer offered is not separation but pardon. Pardon is then set under God's own forgiving. So the model for how to treat a relative who held you back is taken from how God treats you.

crossReferences.why: Uses two of the same three verbs and gives the reason this passage leaves implicit, God's forgiveness of you.
Names the same pair a trial in almost identical words, in a passage about keeping a trust.
Shows the same tension inside a family, resistance on one point and good company on everything else.

studies.applyIt: If someone close to you has stood in the way of something that mattered to you, write down what it cost. Then write down one reason they may have had that was not malice. You do not have to believe it. The ayah names the block and then spends more words on pardon than on the warning. That is the proportion to copy.
studies.explainEasier: Sometimes people in your own family get in the way of what you believe. God says to watch out, but also to forgive them and let it go. He calls your money and your children a test.

studies.title: As Much As You Can
studies.meaning: Four orders come in a row. The first carries a limit the others do not: be mindful of God as much as you are able. Early scholars weigh that phrase with care. They read it as setting the bar at what you can do, not as lowering the bar. Then come hearing, obeying and spending, with a short clause saying the spending is better for you. The ayah closes with a line about being saved from your own grasping. The same line appears earlier in the Quran.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the end of a surah about family, property and what people do under pressure. No set occasion is reported for this ayah. Some early authorities asked how it relates to an earlier order to be mindful of God as He deserves. Most read this one as the same demand, put in terms a person can actually meet. The community it spoke to had little to spare.

keyTerms.note: A verb of having the power or the room for something. The clause measures the demand against the person rather than against a fixed bar, which is why it has been read as a mercy rather than a discount.
Placed before obeying, and kept apart from it. The order implies that hearing is itself an act. Arabic uses this verb for listening in order to comply, not for the ear alone.
The gain is handed to the giver in the same breath as the order to give. Early scholars note the turn: what leaves the hand is said to come back to the one who let it go.
From a root meaning to split open, used of a farmer breaking ground. Success in this word is what comes up after something has been cut into, which suits a clause about giving.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Most households in Medina had very little slack. A family might own a few palms and a goat. Giving meant a measure of dates that would have been eaten. In that setting, a broad order to spend needed the limit that opens the ayah. The people who heard it knew at once that the measure was their own means, not their neighbour's.
studies.didYouKnow: The limit in this ayah, as much as you can, is one of the most quoted phrases in the tradition. It turns an open-ended demand into a personal one. It sits beside the closing line of the longest surah, which says God does not charge a soul beyond what it can bear. The two are usually read together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah sets a demand and a limit in one clause, and that changes what failing means. A person is measured against their own means. So the bar is not lowered for everyone, and it is out of reach for no one. The order of the four instructions matters too. Awareness comes first, hearing and obeying next, giving last. The outward act sits at the end of a chain that starts inside.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle as a fact about God rather than as a qualifier attached to an instruction.
Gives the unqualified version of the same command, which early readers set beside this one.
Follows immediately and reframes the spending as a loan that is returned with increase.

studies.applyIt: Set your standard this week by what you can carry, not by an ideal. Ask what you can actually keep up. Then do that, and stop measuring it against what you think you should manage. The ayah puts the limit inside the command. Falling short of an ideal you invented is not the failure this sentence describes.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to keep him in mind as much as they are able, to listen, to obey, and to give. He says the giving is good for them. Anyone kept safe from his own greed does well.

studies.title: A Loan To The One Who Owns Everything
studies.meaning: The offer is strange on its face: God, who is about to be described as knowing everything and holding all power, invites a loan. The word is the ordinary commercial one, and the adjective attached to it, good, is read by commentators as covering both the source of what is given and the manner of giving. Two returns are named, multiplication and forgiveness, and then two divine names that are unusual together: appreciative and forbearing. One responds to what is given, the other to what is delayed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the surah's closing ayat. The community's expenses were real and continuous: equipping expeditions, receiving new arrivals with nothing, supporting families whose earners had gone. The commentators do not attach an occasion to these two ayat. They note that the surah ends where it began, with names of God, and that the final line is a single ayah of names with no verb at all.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for money lent and expected back, from a root meaning to cut, since a portion is cut from a larger amount. Using it for giving to God makes the transfer temporary by definition.

A divine name built on the word for gratitude, used of God responding to human action. Classical commentators explain it as giving much for little and accepting small acts, rather than as God owing anything.
A name for restraint held by someone with the power to act at once. Placed beside the name of appreciation, it covers the other half of the exchange: what happens when the loan is not made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lending without interest was a real institution in that economy, not an ideal. A man short before harvest borrowed grain from a neighbour and returned the same measure later, and the arrangement held families through bad seasons. It carried risk and no profit, which is exactly why it was an act of standing rather than of business. The vocabulary of this ayah is taken from that practice, where the lender gains nothing except having lent.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about lending God a good loan appears six times in the Quran, spread across five surahs, and each time the return promised is multiplication. The divine name that means appreciative is far rarer: it occurs only four times in the whole Book, and one of those is here, at the close of this surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Calling it a loan does two things at once. It removes the idea of charity as surrender, since a loan is returned, and it removes the idea of the giver's ownership, since you can only lend what belongs to you and the surah has already said what belongs to God. The names that follow hold the passage open. Appreciation says the small act is registered; forbearance says the door does not close when the act is not performed.

crossReferences.why: Asks who will lend God a good loan and promises multiplication many times over.
Joins the good loan to charity from both men and women, with forgiveness added to the return.
Uses the same rare name, appreciative, in a passage about increase given from God's bounty.

studies.applyIt: Give something this week to a person who cannot return it and will not tell anyone. Time counts. Then let it go entirely, without following up on how it landed. The ayah calls the act a loan, which means the return is somebody else's business to arrange. Most of the difficulty in giving is the wish to watch it work.
